title: Delivering Data When Packets Get Lost

sources.title: MIT 16.36 Lecture 18: ARQ Protocols

sections.title: A packet vanishes
sections.narration: Packet one vanishes between sender and receiver. The sender cannot see delivery directly. Watch us add feedback, timers, and sequence state to recover without delivering the same data twice.
bullets: How can it know what arrived?
sections.takeaway: Reliability requires feedback and carefully tracked state.

sections.title: Read the timeline
sections.narration: The sender and receiver remain on opposite sides. Time moves downward. Sloping paths show travel delay; return paths show acknowledgments. Separate sending, arrival, and confirmation as you follow them.
sections.takeaway: A timeline separates transmission, arrival, and acknowledgment events.

sections.title: Send one, then wait
sections.narration: Stop-and-wait permits one outstanding packet. The sender keeps a copy and waits for confirmation before advancing. The saved copy becomes important when something disappears on the path.
sections.takeaway: Stop-and-wait permits one unacknowledged packet at a time.

sections.title: Choose an ACK convention
sections.narration: Our ACK number always means next expected packet. ACK one confirms packet zero; ACK four confirms zero through three. Other numbering conventions exist, so keep this definition consistent.
bullets: ACK n means next expected n
sections.takeaway: Every ACK number here identifies the next packet expected.

sections.title: Notice the idle gap
sections.narration: After transmission finishes, the packet still travels outward and its acknowledgment travels back. The sender waits during that interval. A faster link alone does not remove propagation delay.
sections.takeaway: Long feedback delay can leave a fast link mostly idle.

sections.title: Separate two kinds of time
sections.narration: Transmission time is packet length divided by link rate. Propagation is the signal's travel time. Watch the short sending interval and the much longer round trip occupy different portions.
sections.takeaway: Transmission time and propagation delay measure different things.

sections.title: Calculate stop-and-wait use
sections.narration: Assume one millisecond sending and twenty milliseconds round-trip propagation, ignoring acknowledgment overhead. Useful sending occupies one of twenty-one milliseconds: about four point eight percent of the cycle.
sections.takeaway: With negligible ACK cost, utilization is 1 divided by 21, about 4.8 percent.

sections.title: Lose the data packet
sections.narration: The data packet disappears, so no confirmation returns. The sender still has its copy but cannot tell whether data, feedback, or delay caused the silence. Waiting forever prevents progress.
bullets: No new ACK can confirm it
sections.takeaway: A missing acknowledgment leaves the sender uncertain.

sections.title: Expire a timer
sections.narration: A retransmission timer limits waiting. Expiry means confirmation is missing, not that loss is certain. Delayed traffic can also expire a timer, so recovery must tolerate duplicate arrivals.
sections.takeaway: A timeout detects missing confirmation, not certain packet loss.

sections.title: Retransmit the saved copy
sections.narration: Send the saved packet again with its original sequence number. A successful arrival returns ACK one. Confirmation lets the sender release its copy and move to new data.
sections.takeaway: Retransmission retries the same logical packet.

sections.title: Lose the acknowledgment instead
sections.narration: This time the data arrives, but its acknowledgment disappears. The sender again lacks confirmation and retries. The receiver must recognize that another physical arrival is the same logical data.
sections.takeaway: The sender may retry data that the receiver already has.

sections.title: Recognize the duplicate
sections.narration: The receiver already expects packet one. Another packet zero is a duplicate: do not deliver it again, but repeat ACK one. Count accepted application data separately from physical arrivals.
sections.takeaway: Sequence state distinguishes a duplicate from new data.

sections.title: Why alternating bits can work
sections.narration: A basic stop-and-wait protocol can alternate sequence bits zero and one. Reuse requires assumptions about initialization and old duplicates; our larger example keeps increasing labels for clarity.
sections.takeaway: A small sequence space requires careful assumptions about delayed duplicates.

sections.title: Choose a sensible timeout
sections.narration: A timer that is too short creates unnecessary repeats; one too long delays recovery. Watch a delayed acknowledgment arrive after premature expiry. Practical protocols adapt to changing delay conditions.
sections.takeaway: A timer trades quick recovery against unnecessary retransmission.

sections.title: Allow four packets in flight
sections.narration: Allow four unconfirmed packets instead of one. The window bounds outstanding data while saved copies await acknowledgment. Watch the allowed region expand; it does not create four physical links.
sections.takeaway: A sender window permits several packets before confirmation.

sections.title: Fill the pipeline
sections.narration: Send zero, one, two, and three without stopping after each. Later data travels while earlier feedback returns. This overlap improves utilization when delay would otherwise leave the sender idle.
sections.takeaway: Pipelining overlaps useful transmission with feedback travel.

sections.title: Use cumulative acknowledgments
sections.narration: ACK three means packets zero, one, and two are confirmed in order. One newer cumulative acknowledgment can also cover an earlier lost acknowledgment. A gap still blocks confirmation beyond it.
bullets: An earlier missing ACK may be covered
sections.takeaway: Cumulative ACKs confirm a contiguous prefix of received data.

sections.title: Slide the sending window
sections.narration: In this separate ACK-two example, zero and one leave the outstanding region. The window advances two positions, permitting new transmissions on the right without increasing its fixed size.
sections.takeaway: Acknowledgments advance the window and permit new transmissions.

sections.title: Go-Back-N: lose packet 1
sections.narration: Send zero through three, then lose one. Zero is accepted, and the receiver now expects one. We pause new transmissions so the remaining outstanding set stays one, two, and three.
sections.takeaway: A gap prevents contiguous in-order acceptance in this Go-Back-N model.

sections.title: Discard later arrivals
sections.narration: This basic Go-Back-N receiver discards packets two and three while expecting one. It repeats ACK one. Arriving at the interface is different from being accepted into the contiguous sequence.
sections.takeaway: A basic Go-Back-N receiver discards out-of-order packets.

sections.title: Retransmit from the gap
sections.narration: When the oldest unconfirmed packet times out, retransmit one, two, and three. Confirmed packet zero is not repeated. This simple policy can resend data previously received but discarded.
sections.takeaway: Go-Back-N retransmits outstanding packets starting at the oldest unconfirmed one.

sections.title: Accept the repaired sequence
sections.narration: Now one, two, and three arrive in order. ACK four confirms the repaired prefix, and the sender releases those saved copies. Four is the next expected packet, not the last accepted.
sections.takeaway: Once the gap is repaired, in-order acceptance and window movement resume.

sections.title: Compare the mechanisms carefully
sections.narration: A larger window can keep a delayed link busier, up to its available capacity. Compare windows one, four, and twenty-one. Modern TCP adds byte sequencing and mechanisms beyond this teaching model.
sections.takeaway: Modern TCP is related to ARQ ideas but is not this exact frame protocol.

sections.title: Reconstruct reliability yourself
sections.narration: Feedback confirms progress, timers trigger retries, and sequence state prevents duplicate delivery. Windows overlap travel and useful work. These mechanisms still require eventual successful communication; permanent failure cannot be overcome.
sections.takeaway: Recovery needs feedback and state; permanent link failure can still stop delivery.
